As of 238 PM EDT Thursday...

KEY MESSAGE 1: It's a beautiful fall day out there with chilly 
temperatures running about 5 degrees below normal. Winds are light, 
and the Sun is shining. Today will probably be the last day for 
optimal foliage, because it's going to get breezy and wet for Friday.

Overnight, a warm front will approach the area. Rain chances will 
quickly ramp up as strong ascent from moist air overrunning stable, 
dry high pressure produces a solid precipitation shield northwards. 
After the warm front crosses, conditions will become increasingly 
favorable for gusty winds, particularly in the Champlain Valley. 
Conditions are only marginally favorable for mixing, but the 
orientation of the winds, and channeled flow between low pressure 
reaching Montreal and retreating Atlantic high pressure will favor 
gusty winds in and around Lake Champlain. High res guidance also 
seems to favor northern slopes near Enosburg and Montgomery Center 
in eastern Franklin, as well as East Charleston and Derby Center. 
Climatologically speaking, one cannot rule out areas like Malone and 
Ellenburg in New York either. Within the aforementioned areas, 35 to 
45 mph are most likely from about 7am-1pm. Outside of these, still 
plenty of breezy winds 25-35 mph. Combined with the rain, this will 
almost certainly take away plenty of foliage, and it may be strong 
enough that some localized reports of large branches down and some 
power outages are possible. However, south winds are usually not as 
impactful given how common strong southerly gusts are in the 
Champlain Valley.

By mid-afternoon, the surface low will begin to reach Montreal and 
then shift eastwards. The attendant cold front will push southeast. 
There could be some convective elements and some type of shear line 
that shows up on radar, but instability is marginal and any winds 
within precipitation will likely be lower than the ongoing synoptic 
scale winds. Still, between the strong warm front and some moderate 
rainfall rates likely in the cold front with higher PWATs around 250-
275 percent of normal, we should eke out at least 0.50", even for 
most terrain shadowed locations. Totals are most likely to range 
about 0.75-1.25", especially across higher terrain. No flood 
concerns are expected with the progressive nature of the feature.

KEY MESSAGE 2: Increasingly cool weather returns under northwest flow 
Friday night through the rest of the weekend. The backside of the 
upper trough doesn't shift southeast until later Saturday morning. 
So with lingering moisture, upslope showers are expected. As 
temperatures cool, snow levels will gradually descend as 
temperatures fall into the mid 20s to mid 30s. Some snowflakes may 
manage to even make it to the valley floor if there are any. 
Unblocked flow will generally favor most orographically enhanced 
showers near the summits and along their eastern slopes. Approaching 
noon, snow showers will taper off as moisture flows out of the 
region due to the unblocked flow and upper trough pulling away. Due 
to antecedent warmth, most accumulations will be on grassy surfaces 
for areas between 1000-2500 ft elevation. Above 2500 ft, snowfall 
amounts could approach 1-2".

Temperatures aren't going to warm a whole lot Saturday as brisk 
northwest wind gusts of 25 to 35 mph will remain much of the day. 
Max temperatures will be in the mid 30s to mid 40s. So as winds 
slacken on Saturday night, we should see most all locations fall at 
or below freezing, except for perhaps a handful of spots in Grand 
Isle, Vermont and around the immediate shores of Lake Champlain. 
South to southwest flow will resume on Sunday, and we will moderate 
closer to seasonal norms. The high pressure set up overhead will be 
very strong, and appears unlikely to budge anytime soon. Signals are 
quite good for a dry spell.

KEY MESSAGE 3: Little change was noted in the 12z guidance suite, which 
support expanding mid/upper lvl ridge acrs most of the Great Lakes 
and NE CONUS. Did note a weak moisture-starved backdoor cold front 
on Weds, which may knock our temps back below normal, depending upon 
magnitude of caa. Guidance shows building 1035mb ridge from Maine to 
VA by early next week, while closed cyclonic circulation lingers 
well east of Hatteras. This high pres is replaced by another 1034mb 
high pres over central Canada by mid-week, helping to advect 
slightly cooler temps into our cwa for mid to late week. However 
with very dry moisture profiles only a few sprinkles acrs the trrn 
wl be possible. Temps mostly in the mid 50s to l/m 60s with lows 
upper 20s to lower 40s thru most of the extended with dry conditions 
prevails. Fire weather concerns will increase next week, due to the 
long duration of dry weather anticipated, but winds will remain 
mostly light and terrain driven, with high pres.
